extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in philosophy of mathematics (graduate students, philosophers, advanced undergraduates)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes the standards, methodological maxims, and justificatory criteria that philosophers and practicing mathematicians use to evaluate mathematical objects, axioms (especially in set theory), and ontological proposals (platonism, structuralism, nominalism, fictionalism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maddy’s maxim: unify
rubrics_metrics.description: “unify” — an instigation for set theory to provide a single system in which all mathematical objects and structures of mathematics can be instantiated or modelled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maddy presents 'unify' as a methodological maxim guiding set theorists when contemplating acceptability of new set-theoretic principles: favour principles that increase the unifying power of the theory (i.e., allow many mathematical objects/structures to be represented within one system).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maddy’s maxim: maximize
rubrics_metrics.description: “maximize” — set theory should adopt set theoretic principles that are as powerful and mathematically fruitful as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used (with 'unify') as informal methodological criteria that support taking new axioms if they expand the theory’s strength and yield mathematical fruitfulness; contrasted with views that demand metaphysical truth as the sole guide.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal vs external question standard (Carnap/Tait)
rubrics_metrics.description: Questions of existence of mathematical entities can only be sensibly asked and reasonably answered from within (axiomatic) mathematical frameworks; external/metaphysical questions are illegitimate or meaningless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tait’s deflationary proposal: keep ontological questions 'within the framework' of mathematical practice (e.g., ask whether there are primes with some property inside number theory) and resist supra-mathematical demands for metaphysical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benacerraf’s epistemological challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: Platonistic accounts must explain how we (spatially and temporally localized beings) can have knowledge of non-spatial, non-temporal abstract mathematical entities given standard epistemological theories (e.g., causal theories, reliabilism).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as a constraint on ontologies: a satisfactory philosophical account must offer a plausible epistemology or show how reliable beliefs/reference to mathematical objects are possible despite abstractness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hodes’ semantic/causal-reference challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: The platonist must provide an account of how physically embodied humans are able to refer to abstract mathematical entities, given causal-historical theories of reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hodes’s variant narrows the epistemological problem to a semantic/reference problem: satisfactory theories must supply a plausible 'microstructure of reference' for mathematical discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plenitudinous platonism consistency criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Every logically consistent mathematical theory necessarily refers to an abstract entity (i.e., consistency suffices to posit an abstract referent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On this view (Linsky & Zalta; Balaguer), consistency of a theory is the main requirement for postulating its corresponding mathematical entity; consequences include multiple mathematical universes and indeterminate answers to e.g. continuum hypothesis across universes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictionalism: consistency requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: If mathematical theories are fictional, then a necessary demand is that the mathematical theories be consistent (so the 'stories' don't contain contradictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fictionalists treat mathematics like literature; consistency is needed to avoid triviality and to make mathematical practice viable as a game of make-believe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictionalism: conservativity over natural science
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematics (if fictional) must be conservative over natural science: whenever an empirical statement can be derived using mathematics, it should in principle be derivable without mathematics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Field's additional requirement is designed to block indispensability-style arguments against fictionalism: mathematics must not be essential to deriving empirical conclusions, otherwise fictional entities would be explanatorily indispensable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nominalistic reconstruction requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Nominalist accounts must provide concrete surrogates and concrete relations that simulate the role abstract entities play in scientific and mathematical theories.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful nominalistic reconstructions (e.g., Field’s for Newtonian mechanics) must supply enough concrete entities/structures (e.g., spacetime regions) to play the mathematical roles; limitations include potential finiteness of concrete entities and difficulty simulating higher mathematics or set theory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Putnam’s modal-existential requirement for in rebus nominalism
rubrics_metrics.description: For nominalist structuralism to yield correct truth conditions for analysis: it must be possible that there exists a concrete physical system that can serve as a model for the mathematical theory (Putnam’s modal existential assumption).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Putnam’s modal rendering strengthens the nominalist account by requiring merely that a suitable concrete model be possible (not actual); addresses Hilbert’s worry about lack of actual models and helps avoid vacuous truth for universally quantified sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sensible identity/meaning questions must be structural (Shapiro)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensible identity questions are those that can be asked from within a structure and decided on structural grounds; questions that go beyond a structure (mixing different vocabularies) are category mistakes and thereby senseless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shapiro’s structuralist standard targets Benacerraf’s identification problem: e.g., asking '1 ∈ 3' mixes set-theoretic membership with positions in the natural-number structure and so is illegitimate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structuralist criterion for ontological commitment (ante rem vs in rebus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether structures are ontologically prior abstract entities (ante rem structuralism) or exist only in the concrete systems that instantiate them (in rebus structuralism); this choice affects what counts as acceptable ontology and explanatory commitments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ante rem structuralism treats structures as abstract (and so faces Benacerraf-style epistemology); in rebus (nominalist) structuralism avoids abstract structures but needs accounts of model existence/possibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benacerraf’s identification/anti-reduction constraint
rubrics_metrics.description: Any reductive account that identifies natural numbers (or other mathematical objects) with specific sets must handle the multiplicity of equally plausible set-reductions (e.g., several isomorphic set-theoretic constructions); failure yields arbitrariness and undermines reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This functions as an evaluative constraint on reductionist proposals: successful reductions must explain why one identification is privileged or else abandon reductionism in favour of structuralist/sui generis accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justification modes for axioms: intrinsic vs extrinsic evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms (especially large-cardinal axioms) may be justified by intrinsic evidence (e.g., following from reflection principles, internal conceptual considerations) or by extrinsic evidence (fruitfulness, consequences, connections to other mathematics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy of set theory distinguishes weaker large cardinals (supported by intrinsic motivations like reflection) from stronger ones that currently enjoy mainly extrinsic support; evaluative practice weighs these evidence types in accepting new axioms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reflection principles as intrinsic support
rubrics_metrics.description: Reflection principles, which assert that the universe is so rich it resembles some set-sized initial segment, provide intrinsic evidence in favour of certain large-cardinal principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflection-type motivations are cited as internally grounded conceptual reasons to accept weaker large-cardinal axioms, and play a role in intrinsic justification strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative conception and limitation-of-size as axiom-justifying conceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Two systematic conceptions of sets used to motivate ZFC axioms: the iterative conception (universe generated from empty set via power set) and the limitation-of-size conception (every collection not too large is a set).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different axioms of ZFC find better or worse motivation in the two conceptions (e.g., power set fits iterative conception; restricted comprehension fits limitation-of-size); no uniform conception clearly justifies all of ZFC, so axiom acceptance must be pluralistically evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Community-historical justification for axioms (case study: Axiom of Choice)
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance of axioms (like AC) can be mediated by open and explicit discussion within the mathematical community; historical community debate can surface general reasons for acceptance or rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sociological and methodological factors — community practice, debate, and consensus — serve as one legitimate form of justificatory evidence for adopting axioms, alongside conceptual and technical arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Category-theoretic criterion for foundations: definition up to isomorphism
rubrics_metrics.description: Category theory is attractive as a foundation because mathematical objects there are defined only up to isomorphism, thereby defusing identification problems like Benacerraf’s.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Category theory provides an alternative foundation to set theory: it handles structuralist concerns better (objects-as-positions) though tradeoffs remain (not always as natural for some constructions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Size/proper-class constraint and potentialism about the set-theoretic universe
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize Cantor’s diagonal constraints (no set of all sets); debate whether proper classes are bona fide collections or whether the universe is only potentially infinite (never a completed totality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ontological and methodological positions about sets/classes and potential vs actual infinity affect which principles/quantifications are acceptable in set theory; these metaphysical considerations serve as criteria for acceptable foundational accounts.
